implementation_notes: Go's concurrency primitives are the actor model in miniature: a goroutine owns a piece of state, only channels touch it, and no mutex is needed - the Go blog states the rule as do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating. A constructor returns the send-only channel (the address) and keeps the state unexported; a buffered channel bounds the mailbox and blocks the sender, which is the backpressure policy, while an unbuffered channel turns every send into a rendezvous. What replaces the classic structure: there is no Actor base type, no supervision and no address registry - goroutine plus channel is the whole mechanism, so restart policy and liveness checks must be added by hand.
pitfalls: Sharing the struct (or a pointer to it) defeats the pattern: only the channels may escape; keep fields unexported and hand out the channels.
Mailbox buffering silently changes semantics: an unbuffered send blocks the sender until the actor receives, and an unbounded channel removes backpressure entirely.
A goroutine that panics kills the process unless recovered inside the actor loop, because Go has no supervision tree - the restart policy is your code.
A select with a default branch becomes a hot spin loop; omit the default unless a non-blocking send or drop policy is intended.
